questions.question_text: Which of the following is the widely used definition of sustainable development set out in the 1987 Brundtland Report?

options.A: Development that maximises economic growth while keeping pollution within legal limits
options.B: Development that protects the natural environment by halting all further industrial expansion
options.C: Development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs
options.D: Development that ensures every country reaches the same level of income per head

questions.explanation: The Brundtland Report (Our Common Future) defined sustainable development as meeting present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs. The definition is about balancing needs across generations, not about maximising growth within legal limits. It does not require halting industrial activity, nor does it set a goal of equal income per head between countries.

questions.question_text: The United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (UN SDGs) were adopted by UN member states in 2015. How many goals do they contain?
questions.explanation: There are 17 SDGs, supported by 169 targets, forming the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. Eight was the number of the earlier Millennium Development Goals. The figure of 169 is the number of targets, not goals.

questions.question_text: Which of the following best explains why the UN SDGs are significant for businesses as well as governments?

options.A: They are legally binding on all listed companies and must be reported against in annual accounts
options.B: They replace national law on environmental protection in every UN member state
options.C: They apply only to developing countries, so businesses use them mainly for overseas aid programmes
options.D: They provide a shared global framework that businesses can use to identify and communicate how their activities affect social, environmental and economic priorities

questions.explanation: The SDGs are a voluntary, universal framework agreed by governments, but they are widely used by businesses to align strategy, set targets and communicate their contribution to sustainable development. They are not legally binding on companies and do not override national law. Unlike the earlier Millennium Development Goals, the SDGs apply to all countries, not only developing ones.

questions.question_text: What does the term 'Anthropocene' describe?

options.A: A proposed name for the current period in which human activity has become the dominant influence on the Earth's climate and ecosystems
options.B: A model of business strategy that places people ahead of profit
options.C: The period before industrialisation when human impact on the planet was negligible
options.D: An international agreement on reducing greenhouse gas emissions

questions.explanation: The Anthropocene is a term proposed to describe the era in which humans have become a major force shaping the planet's geology, climate and ecosystems. It is not a business model or a treaty. It describes the opposite of the pre-industrial period, when human influence was much smaller.

questions.question_text: The planetary boundaries framework identifies nine Earth-system processes. What is the main purpose of the framework?

options.A: To define a 'safe operating space' for humanity, beyond which there is an increased risk of large-scale and possibly irreversible environmental change
options.B: To set legally enforceable emission limits for each country
options.C: To measure the minimum social needs, such as food and housing, that every person should have
options.D: To rank countries according to the size of their economies relative to their land area

questions.explanation: The planetary boundaries framework identifies limits for processes such as climate change, biosphere integrity and freshwater use, within which humanity can operate safely. Crossing these boundaries increases the risk of abrupt or irreversible change. The framework is scientific, not legally enforceable, and the social foundation of minimum needs is a feature of Doughnut Economics rather than of planetary boundaries.

questions.question_text: Kate Raworth's 'Doughnut Economics' model has an inner ring and an outer ring. A country provides good healthcare, education and housing for all its citizens but its resource use greatly exceeds the Earth's capacity. How would this country be described using the model?

options.A: It falls short of the social foundation but stays within the ecological ceiling
options.B: It meets the social foundation but overshoots the ecological ceiling
options.C: It is operating within the safe and just space for humanity
options.D: It overshoots the social foundation and falls short of the ecological ceiling

questions.explanation: In Doughnut Economics the inner ring is the social foundation (minimum standards for human wellbeing) and the outer ring is the ecological ceiling (limits on pressure on the planet). Meeting citizens' needs means the social foundation is met, but excessive resource use means the ecological ceiling is overshot. The safe and just space is only achieved when both conditions are satisfied at once.

questions.question_text: A manufacturer of office furniture stops selling chairs and instead leases them to customers. At the end of each lease it takes the chairs back, refurbishes them and re-leases them, and recycles parts that cannot be reused. Which concept does this business model best illustrate?

options.A: The linear 'take-make-dispose' economy
options.B: Degrowth
options.C: The circular economy
options.D: Weak sustainability

questions.explanation: A circular economy keeps products and materials in use at their highest value for as long as possible, designing out waste through reuse, refurbishment and recycling. Product-as-a-service models such as leasing support this because the producer keeps ownership and has an incentive to make durable products. A linear economy disposes of products after use, while degrowth refers to reducing overall economic throughput.

questions.question_text: Under the six-capitals model used in integrated reporting, which pairing of item and type of capital is correct?

options.A: Trust built with local communities and suppliers: social and relationship capital
options.B: Software developed in-house: manufactured capital
options.C: Cash held in the bank: natural capital
options.D: Employees' motivation and ability to innovate: intellectual capital

questions.explanation: The six capitals are financial, manufactured, intellectual, human, social and relationship, and natural. Trust and relationships with communities and suppliers are social and relationship capital. In-house software is intellectual capital, cash is financial capital, and employees' motivation and capabilities are human capital.

questions.question_text: Which statement correctly distinguishes 'weak sustainability' from 'strong sustainability'?

options.A: Weak sustainability applies to small businesses, whereas strong sustainability applies to large listed companies
options.B: Weak sustainability focuses only on social issues, whereas strong sustainability focuses only on environmental issues
options.C: Weak sustainability assumes natural capital can be replaced by other forms of capital, whereas strong sustainability holds that critical natural capital must be preserved because it cannot be substituted
options.D: Weak sustainability requires zero emissions immediately, whereas strong sustainability allows emissions to fall gradually

questions.explanation: The distinction concerns substitutability between forms of capital. Weak sustainability treats total capital as what matters, so a loss of natural capital can be offset by gains in manufactured or financial capital. Strong sustainability holds that some natural capital is critical and non-substitutable, so it must be maintained in its own right. The terms are not about business size, a single pillar, or the speed of emission cuts.

questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes the concept of 'degrowth' as contrasted with 'green growth'?

options.A: Degrowth argues that economies should grow faster to fund environmental clean-up, whereas green growth argues for zero growth
options.B: Degrowth argues for a planned reduction in energy and resource use in high-income economies, whereas green growth argues that economic growth can continue if it is decoupled from environmental harm
options.C: Degrowth and green growth both argue that GDP must fall in every country
options.D: Degrowth refers to falling population, whereas green growth refers to rising population

questions.explanation: Green growth holds that GDP can keep rising while environmental pressures fall, through technology and efficiency that decouple growth from resource use. Degrowth questions whether sufficient decoupling is achievable and proposes a deliberate scaling down of material and energy throughput in wealthy economies, with a focus on wellbeing rather than GDP. Neither concept is about population size.

questions.question_text:
Over a period, a country's GDP rose from £500bn to £600bn and its greenhouse gas emissions rose from 200 million tonnes CO2e to 210 million tonnes CO2e.
Which of the following correctly describes what happened?

options.A: Emissions intensity fell by 12.5%, which is absolute decoupling
options.B: Emissions intensity rose by 5.0%, so there was no decoupling
options.C: Emissions intensity fell by 20.0%, which is relative decoupling only
options.D: Emissions intensity fell by 12.5%, which is relative decoupling only

questions.explanation: Emissions intensity was 200/500 = 0.40 Mt per £bn at the start and 210/600 = 0.35 Mt per £bn at the end. The fall is (0.40 - 0.35) / 0.40 = 12.5% (rounded to one decimal place). Because total emissions still rose, this is relative decoupling; absolute decoupling would require emissions to fall in total while GDP grows. The 5.0% figure is the rise in absolute emissions and 20.0% is the rise in GDP, not the change in intensity.

questions.question_text: Which of the following global sustainability challenges is primarily social and demographic rather than environmental?

options.A: Loss of species due to habitat destruction
options.B: Accumulation of plastic waste in the oceans
options.C: Rapid urbanisation and migration placing pressure on housing and public services
options.D: Rising average global temperatures

questions.explanation: Urbanisation and migration are population trends that mainly affect society, for example through demand for housing, infrastructure and services. Species decline, plastic pollution and rising temperatures are primarily environmental challenges, although all of these issues are interconnected.

questions.question_text: When identifying the key stakeholders in sustainability, why are future generations often described as a particularly challenging stakeholder group?

options.A: They have the greatest economic power over current business decisions
options.B: They are legally entitled to sue companies for damage caused before they were born
options.C: They are already represented on most company boards
options.D: They will bear the consequences of today's decisions but cannot express their views or influence those decisions directly

questions.explanation: Future generations are central to the definition of sustainable development, yet they have no voice in present-day decision-making. Their interests therefore have to be considered through others, such as regulators, NGOs and responsible boards. They have no current economic power and no general legal right to sue, and they are not represented on boards.

questions.question_text: What are the three pillars of sustainability?

options.A: Environmental, legal and technological
options.B: Financial, manufactured and human
options.C: Environmental, social and economic
options.D: Governance, risk and compliance

questions.explanation: The three pillars of sustainability are environmental, social and economic. They reflect the idea that sustainability requires balancing the needs of the planet, people and the economy. Financial, manufactured and human are forms of capital rather than pillars.

questions.question_text: John Elkington's 'triple bottom line' encourages organisations to report on which three areas?

options.A: People, planet and profit
options.B: Price, product and place
options.C: Profit, payroll and pensions
options.D: Planning, performance and procurement

questions.explanation: The triple bottom line asks organisations to measure social (people), environmental (planet) and economic (profit) performance, rather than financial profit alone. The other options are marketing or operational terms with no link to sustainability reporting.

questions.question_text: Several fishing companies share access to the same sea. Each company increases its catch to maximise its own profits, and within a few years fish stocks collapse, harming all of them. Which concept does this illustrate?

options.A: The circular economy
options.B: Relative decoupling
options.C: The tragedy of the commons
options.D: The social licence to operate

questions.explanation: The tragedy of the commons arises when individuals acting in their own short-term interest overuse a shared resource, depleting it to everyone's detriment. It shows how inaction or uncoordinated action damages environmental sustainability and, in turn, economic sustainability. The other concepts do not describe the over-exploitation of a shared resource.

questions.question_text: An audit of a clothing retailer's overseas suppliers finds that workers have had their passports confiscated and are being forced to work excessive hours. Which pillar of sustainability is most directly affected?

options.A: Environmental
options.B: Economic
options.C: Social
options.D: Governance

questions.explanation: Forced labour and the confiscation of identity documents are indicators of modern slavery, a human rights issue that falls under the social pillar. Governance is part of ESG but is not one of the three pillars of sustainability. The issue may have economic consequences for the retailer, but its primary impact is on people.

questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes economic sustainability?

options.A: Maximising profit in the current year regardless of the impact on future periods
options.B: The ability of an economy or organisation to support long-term economic activity and wellbeing without causing damage to the environment or society that undermines that activity
options.C: Ensuring that a company never makes a loss in any financial year
options.D: Keeping prices as low as possible for consumers at all times

questions.explanation: Economic sustainability is about maintaining economic activity and prosperity over the long term, in a way that does not deplete the environmental and social resources on which the economy depends. Short-term profit maximisation can undermine long-term viability. Avoiding any annual loss or minimising prices are not definitions of economic sustainability.

questions.question_text: A chemicals factory discharges waste into a river, harming fishing businesses and communities downstream. The factory does not pay for this harm. In economic terms, what is this an example of?

options.A: A negative externality
options.B: A positive externality
options.C: A sunk cost
options.D: An opportunity cost

questions.explanation: A negative externality is a cost imposed on third parties that is not reflected in the price paid by the producer or consumer. Because the factory does not bear the cost of the pollution, the market under-prices its activity, which is one reason regulation and environmental taxes are used. A positive externality would be a benefit to third parties.

questions.question_text: A government plans to close coal mines to reduce emissions. It also funds retraining for miners and investment in new industries in mining towns. Which concept does this approach reflect?

options.A: Greenwashing
options.B: Weak sustainability
options.C: A just transition
options.D: Offshoring

questions.explanation: A just transition means moving to a low-carbon economy in a way that is fair to workers and communities affected by the change. It recognises that environmental action has social and economic consequences, which must be managed. Retraining and regional investment address the social pillar alongside the environmental goal.

questions.question_text: Which of the following best illustrates the interconnection between the three pillars of sustainability?

options.A: A company changes its auditor after a tender process
options.B: Prolonged drought causes crop failures, which raise food prices and push vulnerable households into poverty
options.C: A government increases the basic rate of income tax by one percentage point
options.D: A retailer launches a new website to sell its products online

questions.explanation: The drought is an environmental event that leads to an economic effect (higher food prices) and a social effect (increased poverty), showing how the pillars are linked. The other options describe events that do not demonstrate a chain of effects across the environmental, social and economic pillars.

questions.question_text: A company announces that it will pay all staff at least a 'living wage' rather than the legal minimum wage. How does a living wage differ from a minimum wage?

options.A: A living wage is based on the income needed to cover a basic but acceptable standard of living, whereas a minimum wage is the legal floor set by law
options.B: A living wage is a legal requirement, whereas a minimum wage is voluntary
options.C: A living wage applies only to directors, whereas a minimum wage applies to other employees
options.D: A living wage is always lower than the minimum wage

questions.explanation: A living wage is a voluntary benchmark calculated from the cost of meeting basic needs, and is typically higher than the statutory minimum. The minimum wage is the legal floor that employers must pay. Paying a living wage supports social sustainability by reducing in-work poverty.

questions.question_text: Which statement best explains why delaying action on climate change can damage economic sustainability?

options.A: Delay always reduces costs because technology will make all future action free
options.B: Delay has no economic effect because climate change is solely an environmental issue
options.C: Delay improves economic sustainability because it avoids any spending on low-carbon investment
options.D: Delay tends to increase the eventual costs of adaptation and of a faster, more disruptive transition, and raises the risk of assets losing value before the end of their expected lives

questions.explanation: The longer action is delayed, the greater the physical damage that must be adapted to and the sharper the policy changes needed later, both of which raise costs. A sudden transition can leave carbon-intensive assets stranded, damaging investors and the wider economy. Climate change is not purely environmental, and avoiding investment now does not remove the costs; it defers and usually increases them.

questions.question_text: The Gini coefficient is a common measure of economic inequality within a country. What does a Gini coefficient of zero indicate?

options.A: Perfect inequality, with one person receiving all the income
options.B: That the economy has zero growth
options.C: That the country has no unemployment
options.D: Perfect equality, with income shared equally by everyone

questions.explanation: The Gini coefficient ranges from 0 (perfect equality) to 1, or 100 if expressed as a percentage (perfect inequality). It measures how income or wealth is distributed, not growth or unemployment. Rising inequality is one of the key challenges to social and economic sustainability.

questions.question_text: Some sustainability models present the three pillars as three overlapping circles of equal size, while others present them as nested circles, with the economy inside society and society inside the environment. What is the main point made by the nested model?

options.A: The economy depends on society, and both depend on the environment, so environmental limits constrain the other two pillars
options.B: Each pillar is independent, so trade-offs between them are never needed
options.C: The economy is the largest system and the environment is a small part of it
options.D: Social issues are irrelevant once environmental targets are achieved

questions.explanation: The nested model emphasises that the economy exists within society and that both rely on the natural environment. This means economic activity cannot be sustained if it breaches environmental limits, a view associated with strong sustainability. The overlapping-circles model treats the pillars as more equal and allows trade-offs, which the nested model challenges.

questions.question_text: A mining company has the legal permits it needs, but local communities strongly oppose its new mine and have organised blockades. Which concept best describes what the company lacks?

options.A: A social licence to operate
options.B: Planning permission
options.C: A going concern basis
options.D: Limited liability

questions.explanation: A social licence to operate is the ongoing acceptance of a company's activities by local communities and other stakeholders. It is not a legal document, so a company can have all permits yet still lack community support. Losing it can lead to delays, protests and reputational damage, showing how social sustainability affects business viability.

questions.question_text: A government is choosing between making climate disclosures mandatory by law and issuing voluntary guidance. Which of the following is an advantage of mandatory regulation over voluntary guidance?

options.A: It is always cheaper for companies to comply with than voluntary guidance
options.B: It improves consistency and comparability, because all entities in scope must report and cannot choose only favourable information
options.C: It can be changed more quickly than guidance in response to new developments
options.D: It allows each company to choose which topics to report on

questions.explanation: Mandatory regulation creates a level playing field because every entity in scope must comply, which improves comparability and reduces selective reporting. However, it typically raises compliance costs and is slower to change than guidance. Letting companies choose their topics is a feature of voluntary approaches.

questions.question_text: What is the central long-term temperature goal of the Paris Agreement adopted in 2015?

options.A: To return global average temperature to pre-industrial levels by 2030
options.B: To limit the increase in global average temperature to 3°C above current levels
options.C: To ensure that developed countries reduce emissions while developing countries make no commitments
options.D: To hold the increase in global average temperature to well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels and to pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5°C

questions.explanation: The Paris Agreement aims to keep warming well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels while pursuing efforts to limit it to 1.5°C. Countries set their own nationally determined contributions (NDCs) and all parties participate, unlike the earlier Kyoto Protocol, which placed binding targets mainly on developed countries.

questions.question_text: What is the main role of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC)?

options.A: To assess and summarise the scientific evidence on climate change for policymakers
options.B: To set legally binding emission limits for each country
options.C: To issue sustainability reporting standards for listed companies
options.D: To fine companies that exceed their emission allowances

questions.explanation: The IPCC is a UN body that assesses published research on climate change, its impacts and possible responses, and produces assessment reports for policymakers. It does not set binding limits, write reporting standards or enforce penalties. Its reports inform international negotiations under the UN climate framework.

questions.question_text: The UN Global Compact asks businesses to commit to ten principles. These principles cover which four areas?

options.A: Human rights, labour, environment and anti-corruption
options.B: Profit, growth, innovation and market share
options.C: Audit, tax, financial reporting and assurance
options.D: Health, education, housing and transport

questions.explanation: The UN Global Compact is a voluntary initiative under which companies commit to ten principles in the areas of human rights, labour, environment and anti-corruption. It is an example of an international organisation driving change through voluntary commitment rather than law.

questions.question_text: Under a 'cap-and-trade' emissions trading scheme, how is the cost of emitting greenhouse gases created?

options.A: A limit is set on total emissions, allowances are issued up to that limit, and companies that emit more than their allowances must buy more from those that emit less
options.B: Every company pays a fixed tax per tonne of emissions set by the government, with no overall limit
options.C: Companies receive subsidies for each tonne of emissions they produce
options.D: Companies are banned from emitting any greenhouse gases at all

questions.explanation: Cap-and-trade sets an overall cap on emissions and creates tradeable allowances. The market price of allowances puts a cost on emissions and rewards companies that cut emissions cheaply, as they can sell surplus allowances. A fixed charge per tonne without a cap describes a carbon tax instead.

questions.question_text: CDP (formerly the Carbon Disclosure Project) is a non-governmental organisation. How does it mainly drive sustainability change?

options.A: By passing legislation that requires companies to report emissions
options.B: By acting as the statutory auditor of company sustainability reports
options.C: By running a global disclosure system through which companies, cities and others report environmental data, which investors and customers can use
options.D: By issuing accounting standards for financial statements

questions.explanation: CDP is an NGO that collects environmental disclosures on climate, water and forests and makes them available to investors and purchasers. Its influence comes from transparency and stakeholder pressure, not from law. NGOs cannot legislate, act as statutory auditors or set financial reporting standards.

questions.question_text: The EU Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) requires in-scope companies to report using the European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS). Which materiality concept underpins the CSRD?

options.A: Financial materiality only, considering just the effects of sustainability matters on the company
options.B: Impact materiality only, ignoring effects on the company's finances
options.C: Double materiality, considering both the company's impacts on people and the environment and the sustainability matters that affect the company's financial position
options.D: Quantitative materiality, set at a fixed percentage of profit before tax

questions.explanation: The CSRD is an example of sustainability goals being codified into law, and it uses double materiality. A matter is material if it is material from an impact perspective (inside-out), a financial perspective (outside-in), or both. This differs from the ISSB standards, which focus on financial materiality for investors.

questions.question_text: The recommendations of the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD) were originally voluntary. Which statement best illustrates the trend from less prescriptive guidance to more codified regulation?

options.A: The TCFD recommendations were withdrawn because no companies used them
options.B: The TCFD recommendations were turned into a voluntary charity pledge with no reporting requirements
options.C: The TCFD recommendations were built into the ISSB's IFRS S2 standard, which jurisdictions can then make mandatory for companies through law or listing rules
options.D: The TCFD recommendations replaced all financial reporting standards

questions.explanation: The TCFD framework, structured around governance, strategy, risk management and metrics and targets, began as voluntary guidance. Its structure was incorporated into IFRS S2 Climate-related Disclosures, and jurisdictions can adopt the ISSB standards as mandatory requirements. This shows the move from voluntary guidance to codified, enforceable standards.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is an external influence on a company's sustainability strategy?

options.A: The company's own internal recycling policy
options.B: Investors asking for evidence of how the company manages climate-related risks
options.C: The personal hobbies of the finance director
options.D: The colour scheme of the company's head office

questions.explanation: Investor pressure is an external influence that can shape strategy, along with customers, regulators, competitors and wider society. An internal recycling policy is a result of strategy rather than an external influence, and the other options are irrelevant to sustainability strategy.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a common barrier to progress in corporate sustainability?

options.A: Strong demand from customers for sustainable products
options.B: Short-termism, where management focuses on quarterly or annual results at the expense of long-term investment
options.C: Clear and reliable sustainability data
options.D: Government grants for low-carbon investment

questions.explanation: Short-termism discourages investment whose benefits arrive in the long term, which is typical of many sustainability initiatives. Other barriers include upfront costs, lack of reliable data and lack of skills. Customer demand, good data and grants are enablers rather than barriers.

questions.question_text: A fruit grower relies on wild bees to pollinate its orchards. In sustainability terms, how is this best described?

options.A: An impact on nature
options.B: A transition risk
options.C: A dependency on nature
options.D: A Scope 3 emission

questions.explanation: A dependency is a reliance on natural, social or other resources that a business needs to operate, such as pollination services. An impact is the effect the business has on people or the environment. If bee populations declined, this dependency would create a risk for the grower, showing how dependencies can lead to risks.

questions.question_text: A warehouse company faces two climate-related risks: (1) its site is increasingly likely to be flooded in severe storms, and (2) average summer temperatures are gradually rising, increasing cooling costs. How should these risks be classified?

options.A: (1) Chronic physical risk; (2) acute physical risk
options.B: (1) Transition risk; (2) acute physical risk
options.C: (1) Acute physical risk; (2) chronic physical risk
options.D: (1) Acute physical risk; (2) transition risk

questions.explanation: Physical risks arise from the physical effects of climate change. Acute physical risks are event-driven, such as storms and floods, whereas chronic physical risks result from longer-term shifts, such as rising average temperatures. Transition risks arise from the move to a low-carbon economy, such as policy or market changes.

questions.question_text: A government introduces a new carbon tax that significantly increases the operating costs of a cement manufacturer. What type of climate-related risk is this?

options.A: Acute physical risk
options.B: Transition risk (policy and legal)
options.C: Chronic physical risk
options.D: Credit risk

questions.explanation: Transition risks arise from policy, legal, technology, market and reputational changes as the economy moves towards lower emissions. A new carbon tax is a policy change, so it is a policy and legal transition risk. It is not caused by the physical effects of climate change.

questions.question_text: A logistics company replaces its diesel vans with electric vehicles and finds that its fuel and maintenance costs fall. Which type of sustainability-related outcome is this?

options.A: A physical risk
options.B: A dependency
options.C: Greenwashing
options.D: An opportunity arising from resource efficiency

questions.explanation: Sustainability is not only about risk; it also creates opportunities such as lower costs through resource efficiency, new products and markets, and improved resilience. Lower running costs from cleaner vehicles are an opportunity. The change does not involve misleading claims, so it is not greenwashing.

questions.question_text: Which statement best describes the difference between the effect of sustainability matters on 'enterprise value' and on 'social value'?

options.A: Enterprise value refers only to charitable donations, whereas social value refers to share price
options.B: Enterprise value and social value are identical, so a company that increases one always increases the other
options.C: Enterprise value effects concern how sustainability matters affect the company's cash flows and value to investors, whereas social value concerns the company's effects on people, society and the environment
options.D: Enterprise value concerns the company's effect on employees, whereas social value concerns its effect on shareholders

questions.explanation: Effects on enterprise value are the 'outside-in' effects of sustainability matters on a company's prospects, which is the focus of investor-oriented reporting. Social value reflects the 'inside-out' impacts of the company on society and the environment. The two often interact, for example when harmful impacts lead to regulation or reputational damage, but they are not identical.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the defining feature of a green bond?

options.A: The money raised must be used to finance projects with environmental benefits
options.B: The interest rate is always lower than on government bonds
options.C: The bond can only be bought by charities
options.D: The bond has no repayment date

questions.explanation: Green bonds are 'use of proceeds' instruments: the funds raised are earmarked for eligible environmental projects, such as renewable energy or energy efficiency. They are typically supported by reporting on how the proceeds were spent. Their pricing, investor base and maturity are not what define them.

questions.question_text: A company takes out a sustainability-linked loan. Which feature distinguishes it from a green loan?

options.A: The loan can only be spent on specific environmental projects
options.B: The loan can be used for general purposes, but its interest rate varies depending on whether the company meets pre-agreed sustainability performance targets
options.C: The loan is interest-free provided that the company publishes a sustainability report
options.D: The loan must be repaid immediately if the company makes a loss

questions.explanation: Sustainability-linked loans link the borrowing cost to the borrower's performance against sustainability KPIs, such as emission reductions, rather than restricting how the money is spent. Green loans, like green bonds, restrict the use of proceeds to eligible green projects. Neither type is interest-free or automatically repayable on making a loss.

questions.question_text: A company commissions a life cycle assessment (LCA) of a product on a 'cradle-to-grave' basis. What will the assessment cover?

options.A: Only the emissions from the company's own factory
options.B: Only the impacts arising after the customer buys the product
options.C: The financial profitability of the product over its life
options.D: Environmental impacts from raw material extraction through manufacture, distribution and use, to final disposal

questions.explanation: Cradle-to-grave LCA covers every stage of a product's life, from extracting raw materials to disposal. A narrower 'cradle-to-gate' assessment stops when the product leaves the factory. LCA measures environmental impacts, not profitability.

questions.question_text: A drinks company is deciding whether to switch from glass bottles to a lighter plastic alternative. Why is a life cycle assessment particularly useful for this decision?

options.A: It guarantees that the cheaper option is also the more sustainable one
options.B: It removes the need to consider any social impacts of the decision
options.C: It only measures impacts at the point of sale, so it is quick to complete
options.D: It can reveal whether reducing impacts at one stage, such as transport, simply shifts greater impacts to another stage, such as disposal

questions.explanation: LCA looks at the whole life of a product, so it helps identify 'burden shifting', where an improvement at one stage creates larger problems elsewhere. Lighter packaging may cut transport emissions but increase waste or pollution at end of life. LCA does not guarantee cost savings and does not replace consideration of social impacts.

questions.question_text: A company tracks three measures: (1) water consumption, (2) employee injury rates and (3) the proportion of independent non-executive directors on the board. How would these be classified under ESG?

options.A: (1) Social; (2) Environmental; (3) Governance
options.B: (1) Environmental; (2) Social; (3) Governance
options.C: (1) Environmental; (2) Governance; (3) Social
options.D: (1) Governance; (2) Social; (3) Environmental

questions.explanation: Water use is an environmental measure, employee health and safety is a social measure, and board independence is a governance measure. ESG factors are commonly used by investors and others to assess how a company manages sustainability-related matters.

questions.question_text: Two ESG rating agencies give the same company very different ratings. Which of the following is the most likely explanation?

options.A: One agency must have made an arithmetic error, as ESG ratings are calculated using a single global standard
options.B: ESG ratings are based only on share price, which varies between stock exchanges
options.C: ESG ratings are set by the company itself, so they can choose any score
options.D: The agencies use different methodologies, including different choices of which issues to measure, how to measure them and how to weight them

questions.explanation: There is no single standard methodology for ESG ratings, so agencies differ in scope, measurement and weighting, and in the data they use. This divergence means users should understand what a rating measures before relying on it. Ratings are not based purely on share price and are not set by the company.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the clearest example of greenwashing?

options.A: A company labels a product 'eco-friendly' because its packaging is recyclable, although the product itself is made using highly polluting processes
options.B: A company publishes verified data showing a fall in its emissions
options.C: A company discloses that it missed its emissions target and explains why
options.D: A company obtains independent assurance over its sustainability report

questions.explanation: Greenwashing is making misleading claims about environmental credentials, for example by highlighting a minor positive feature while ignoring significant negative impacts. Verified data, honest disclosure of missed targets and independent assurance all improve transparency and reduce the risk of greenwashing.

questions.question_text: A company has made real progress in reducing its emissions but decides to say nothing about it publicly because it fears criticism if it misses future targets. What is this practice called?

options.A: Greenwashing
options.B: Carbon offsetting
options.C: Double materiality
options.D: Greenhushing

questions.explanation: Greenhushing is deliberately under-reporting or staying silent about sustainability performance or goals, often to avoid scrutiny. While less obviously harmful than greenwashing, it reduces transparency and makes it harder for stakeholders to assess performance and compare companies.

questions.question_text:
A company reported total greenhouse gas emissions of 18,400 tonnes CO2e for the year and revenue of £230 million.
What is its emissions intensity, measured in tonnes CO2e per £1 million of revenue?

options.A: 0.0125 tonnes CO2e per £1 million
options.B: 800 tonnes CO2e per £1 million
options.C: 80 tonnes CO2e per £1 million
options.D: 8 tonnes CO2e per £1 million

questions.explanation: Emissions intensity = total emissions / revenue in £ millions = 18,400 / 230 = 80 tonnes CO2e per £1 million of revenue. Dividing revenue by emissions gives the inverse figure of 0.0125, which is not an intensity measure. Intensity ratios allow comparison between companies of different sizes, but they can fall even when absolute emissions rise.

questions.question_text: An oil company owns reserves that it may never be able to extract and sell profitably because of tighter climate regulation and falling demand. What term describes these reserves?

options.A: Contingent liabilities
options.B: Natural capital dependencies
options.C: Intangible assets
options.D: Stranded assets

questions.explanation: Stranded assets are assets that suffer unexpected or premature write-downs or devaluations, often because of the transition to a low-carbon economy. They are a key consequence of transition risk and are relevant to the valuation of companies in carbon-intensive sectors.

questions.question_text:
A company set a target to reduce its emissions by 42% from a baseline of 50,000 tonnes CO2e. Its emissions for the current year are 38,500 tonnes CO2e.
By how many further tonnes CO2e must emissions fall from the current level to meet the target?

options.A: 9,500 tonnes CO2e
options.B: 11,500 tonnes CO2e
options.C: 21,000 tonnes CO2e
options.D: 16,170 tonnes CO2e

questions.explanation: The target level is 50,000 x (1 - 0.42) = 29,000 tonnes CO2e. The further reduction needed is 38,500 - 29,000 = 9,500 tonnes CO2e. The figure of 11,500 is the reduction already achieved (50,000 - 38,500), 21,000 is the total reduction required from the baseline, and 16,170 wrongly applies the 42% to the current year's emissions.

questions.topic: The role of the professional accountant in sustainability
questions.question_text: The International Sustainability Standards Board (ISSB) has issued IFRS S1 and IFRS S2. What is the main difference between them?

options.A: IFRS S1 sets general requirements for disclosing sustainability-related financial information, whereas IFRS S2 sets specific requirements for climate-related disclosures
options.B: IFRS S1 covers climate, whereas IFRS S2 covers human rights
options.C: IFRS S1 applies to listed companies, whereas IFRS S2 applies to charities
options.D: IFRS S1 sets assurance requirements, whereas IFRS S2 sets audit fees

questions.explanation: IFRS S1 General Requirements for Disclosure of Sustainability-related Financial Information is the overarching standard. IFRS S2 Climate-related Disclosures deals specifically with climate-related risks and opportunities. Neither standard sets assurance requirements, which are a matter for assurance standard-setters and regulators.

questions.topic: The role of the professional accountant in sustainability
questions.question_text: Who are the primary users of sustainability disclosures prepared under the ISSB standards?

options.A: Local communities affected by the entity's operations
options.B: Employees deciding whether to join a trade union
options.C: Investors, lenders and other creditors making decisions about providing resources to the entity
options.D: Government tax authorities assessing corporation tax

questions.explanation: The ISSB standards focus on information that could reasonably be expected to affect the entity's prospects, and their primary users are investors, lenders and other creditors. This is a financial materiality perspective. Frameworks such as GRI, by contrast, address a wider range of stakeholders and focus on an entity's impacts.

questions.topic: The role of the professional accountant in sustainability
questions.question_text: IFRS S2, building on the TCFD recommendations, organises climate-related disclosures around four core content areas. Which of the following lists them correctly?

options.A: Environment, social, governance and economics
options.B: Governance, strategy, risk management, and metrics and targets
options.C: Planning, doing, checking and acting
options.D: Scope 1, Scope 2, Scope 3 and Scope 4

questions.explanation: The four core content areas are governance, strategy, risk management, and metrics and targets. They are designed to show how an entity oversees, plans for, manages and measures climate-related risks and opportunities. ESG is a broader classification, and the GHG Protocol has only three scopes.

questions.topic: The role of the professional accountant in sustainability
questions.question_text: Under the Greenhouse Gas Protocol, how are emissions from the generation of electricity that a company buys from the national grid classified in the company's own inventory?

options.A: Scope 2
options.B: Scope 1
options.C: Scope 3
options.D: They are excluded because the company does not generate the electricity

questions.explanation: Scope 2 covers indirect emissions from the generation of purchased electricity, steam, heating and cooling consumed by the reporting company. Scope 1 covers direct emissions from sources the company owns or controls, and Scope 3 covers all other indirect emissions in the value chain.

questions.topic: The role of the professional accountant in sustainability
questions.question_text:
A manufacturer identifies the following emission sources:
(1) Gas burned in its own factory boilers
(2) Flights taken by staff on business trips with commercial airlines
(3) Emissions from customers using its products
How should these be classified under the GHG Protocol?

options.A: (1) Scope 1; (2) Scope 2; (3) Scope 3
options.B: (1) Scope 2; (2) Scope 3; (3) Scope 1
options.C: (1) Scope 1; (2) Scope 1; (3) Scope 3
options.D: (1) Scope 1; (2) Scope 3; (3) Scope 3

questions.explanation: Burning gas in the company's own boilers is a direct emission from an owned source, so it is Scope 1. Business travel on commercial airlines and the use of sold products are both indirect value chain emissions, so they are Scope 3. Scope 2 is limited to purchased energy such as electricity.

questions.topic: The role of the professional accountant in sustainability
questions.question_text:
A company reports the following greenhouse gas emissions for the year, in tonnes CO2e:
Scope 1: 4,200
Scope 2: 2,600
Scope 3: 31,200
What are its combined Scope 1 and 2 emissions, and what percentage of its total emissions comes from Scope 3?

options.A: 6,800 tonnes CO2e; 17.9%
options.B: 38,000 tonnes CO2e; 82.1%
options.C: 6,800 tonnes CO2e; 82.1%
options.D: 35,800 tonnes CO2e; 87.2%

questions.explanation: Scope 1 and 2 combined = 4,200 + 2,600 = 6,800 tonnes CO2e. Total emissions = 6,800 + 31,200 = 38,000 tonnes CO2e. Scope 3 share = 31,200 / 38,000 x 100 = 82.1% (rounded to one decimal place). The figure of 17.9% is the Scope 1 and 2 share, which shows why value chain emissions often dominate a company's footprint.

questions.topic: The role of the professional accountant in sustainability
questions.question_text:
A transport company used 120,000 litres of diesel in its own lorries during the year. Assume an emission factor of 2.5 kg CO2e per litre of diesel.
What are the resulting emissions in tonnes CO2e, and in which scope are they reported?

options.A: 300 tonnes CO2e, Scope 2
options.B: 300 tonnes CO2e, Scope 1
options.C: 300,000 tonnes CO2e, Scope 1
options.D: 48 tonnes CO2e, Scope 3

questions.explanation: Emissions = 120,000 litres x 2.5 kg CO2e = 300,000 kg CO2e, which is 300,000 / 1,000 = 300 tonnes CO2e. Fuel burned in vehicles the company owns or controls is a direct emission, so it is Scope 1. The 300,000 figure fails to convert kilograms to tonnes, and 48 wrongly divides litres by the factor before converting.

questions.topic: The role of the professional accountant in sustainability
questions.question_text: A practitioner is engaged to provide assurance on a company's sustainability report. How does a limited assurance conclusion typically differ from a reasonable assurance conclusion?

options.A: A limited assurance conclusion gives absolute certainty, whereas reasonable assurance gives none
options.B: A limited assurance conclusion requires more evidence than a reasonable assurance conclusion
options.C: A limited assurance conclusion is given only by the company's own finance team
options.D: A limited assurance conclusion is expressed negatively (nothing has come to our attention to indicate material misstatement), whereas a reasonable assurance conclusion is expressed positively

questions.explanation: In a limited assurance engagement, the practitioner performs fewer procedures and gives a negatively worded conclusion. Reasonable assurance involves more extensive work and a positive opinion, similar to a financial statement audit. Neither gives absolute certainty, and both are given by an independent practitioner.

questions.topic: The role of the professional accountant in sustainability
questions.question_text: Why are professional accountants well placed to provide assurance on sustainability information?

options.A: They are the only professionals legally allowed to measure greenhouse gas emissions
options.B: They do not need to consider ethical requirements on non-financial engagements
options.C: They have skills in evaluating evidence, internal controls and data, and are bound by ethical requirements including independence and professional scepticism
options.D: They can rely entirely on management's representations without further testing

questions.explanation: Assurance skills such as planning, risk assessment, testing controls, gathering evidence and applying professional scepticism transfer well to sustainability information. Ethical requirements, including independence, apply to sustainability assurance engagements just as they do to audits. Accountants may need to work with subject-matter experts, such as engineers or scientists, where specialist knowledge is needed.

questions.topic: The role of the professional accountant in sustainability
questions.question_text: The Global Reporting Initiative (GRI) Standards are widely used for sustainability reporting. What is their main focus?

options.A: Only the effect of climate change on the organisation's cash flows
options.B: The calculation of corporation tax liabilities
options.C: The organisation's most significant impacts on the economy, the environment and people, for a broad range of stakeholders
options.D: The presentation of the statement of financial position

questions.explanation: The GRI Standards are based on impact materiality, focusing on an organisation's impacts on the economy, environment and people, including human rights. They are aimed at a wide range of stakeholders. This contrasts with the ISSB's investor-focused, financial materiality approach, and the two can be used together.

questions.topic: The role of the professional accountant in sustainability
questions.question_text: Which of the following is a role played by professional accountancy bodies such as ICAEW in driving sustainability?

options.A: Including sustainability in professional qualifications and providing guidance and resources to members
options.B: Passing national sustainability legislation
options.C: Setting legally binding emission caps for companies
options.D: Running national electricity grids

questions.explanation: Accountancy bodies drive sustainability by educating students, supporting members with guidance and CPD, contributing to standard-setting consultations and advocating for change. They do not pass legislation or set legally binding emission limits, which are the role of governments and regulators.

questions.topic: The role of the professional accountant in sustainability
questions.question_text: Which of the following is an example of a professional accountant adopting a sustainable approach within their own workplace?

options.A: Using secure remote access and video calls to review client records where a site visit is not necessary, reducing travel
options.B: Printing every working paper in colour so that it is easier to read
options.C: Driving to every client meeting regardless of distance
options.D: Keeping all office equipment switched on overnight

questions.explanation: Professional accountants can reduce their own environmental impact through choices such as cutting unnecessary travel, reducing paper use and saving energy. Remote working must still meet professional requirements, such as obtaining sufficient evidence and protecting confidential data.

questions.topic: The role of the professional accountant in sustainability
questions.question_text:
A management accountant is appraising a project expected to generate annual net cash inflows of £500,000 before any carbon cost. The project will emit 2,000 tonnes CO2e per year. The company applies an internal (shadow) carbon price of £80 per tonne in investment appraisal.
What annual net cash inflow should be used in the appraisal after applying the internal carbon price?
questions.explanation: The annual carbon cost = 2,000 tonnes x £80 = £160,000. Adjusted annual net cash inflow = £500,000 - £160,000 = £340,000. Using an internal carbon price helps the company anticipate future carbon costs and avoid investing in projects that could become uneconomic. Adding the cost (£660,000) or deducting only £80 (£499,920) are errors.

questions.topic: The concept of ethics and its significance for the accountancy profession
questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes professional ethics?

options.A: The personal moral beliefs an individual developed during childhood
options.B: The laws that apply to all citizens in a country
options.C: The values set out in a company's marketing slogan
options.D: The principles and standards of behaviour expected of members of a profession in carrying out their work

questions.explanation: Professional ethics are the standards of conduct that a profession expects of its members, such as those set out in the ICAEW Code of Ethics. Personal ethics are an individual's own values, and business ethics concern how organisations behave. Law and ethics overlap but are not the same.

questions.topic: The concept of ethics and its significance for the accountancy profession
questions.question_text: Which statement correctly contrasts ethical objectivism with ethical relativism?

options.A: Objectivism holds that ethics depends on the outcome of actions, whereas relativism holds that ethics depends on rules
options.B: Objectivism holds that some moral truths apply universally regardless of culture, whereas relativism holds that what is right depends on the culture or individual
options.C: Objectivism holds that there are no moral truths, whereas relativism holds that all cultures share the same values
options.D: Objectivism applies only to accountants, whereas relativism applies only to lawyers

questions.explanation: Ethical objectivism holds that there are universal moral standards that apply to everyone. Ethical relativism holds that moral standards vary between cultures or individuals, so no single standard is universally correct. Focusing on outcomes versus rules is the distinction between teleological and deontological approaches.

questions.topic: The concept of ethics and its significance for the accountancy profession
questions.question_text: A finance manager refuses to backdate a contract, even though doing so would help the company meet a target and harm no-one, because she believes that misrepresenting facts is wrong in itself. Which ethical approach is she applying?

options.A: Deontological ethics
options.B: Teleological ethics
options.C: Utilitarianism
options.D: Ethical relativism

questions.explanation: Deontological ethics judges actions according to duties and rules, regardless of their consequences. The manager regards misrepresentation as wrong in itself, even if the outcome seems harmless. Teleological approaches, including utilitarianism, would instead focus on the consequences of the action.

questions.topic: The concept of ethics and its significance for the accountancy profession
questions.question_text: Which of the following statements best describes teleological (consequentialist) ethics?

options.A: An action is right if it follows a fixed rule, whatever its results
options.B: An action is right if it is permitted by law
options.C: An action is judged right or wrong according to its outcomes
options.D: An action is right if the person carrying it out feels comfortable about it

questions.explanation: Teleological, or consequentialist, ethics evaluates the morality of an action by its consequences. Utilitarianism is the best-known form. Judging an action by whether it follows rules is deontological, and legality alone does not determine whether an action is ethical.

questions.topic: The concept of ethics and its significance for the accountancy profession
questions.question_text:
A company must choose one of three options. Its analysis of the effect on stakeholders, in units of wellbeing, is:
Option 1: 300 people each gain 2 units; 40 people each lose 10 units
Option 2: 100 people each gain 5 units; 10 people each lose 20 units
Option 3: 50 people each gain 8 units; 200 people each lose 1 unit
Which option would a strict utilitarian choose?

options.A: Option 1
options.B: Option 3
options.C: Option 2
options.D: None, because utilitarianism ignores consequences

questions.explanation: Utilitarianism chooses the action that produces the greatest total net benefit. Option 1: (300 x 2) - (40 x 10) = 200. Option 2: (100 x 5) - (10 x 20) = 300. Option 3: (50 x 8) - (200 x 1) = 200. Option 2 has the highest net benefit of 300 units. Option 1 benefits the most people, but utilitarianism compares total net welfare, not the number of people who gain.

questions.topic: The concept of ethics and its significance for the accountancy profession
questions.question_text: A company legally moves its profits to a low-tax jurisdiction through an artificial arrangement that has no commercial purpose. Many stakeholders criticise the company. What does this illustrate about the relationship between ethics and law?

options.A: Anything that is legal is automatically ethical
options.B: An action can be legal but still be considered unethical
options.C: Ethics only applies where there is no relevant law
options.D: Unethical actions are always illegal

questions.explanation: Law sets minimum standards of behaviour, whereas ethics is about doing the right thing in the circumstances. An arrangement may comply with the letter of the law yet be seen as unfair or contrary to the spirit of the law. Ethical behaviour therefore often goes beyond legal compliance.

questions.topic: The concept of ethics and its significance for the accountancy profession
questions.question_text: Which statement best describes the relationship between ethics and sustainability?

options.A: Sustainability is a purely technical issue with no ethical dimension
options.B: Acting sustainably is part of behaving ethically, because it involves considering the effects of decisions on others, including future generations
options.C: Ethics concerns only individuals, whereas sustainability concerns only governments
options.D: A company can only be ethical if it ignores sustainability to maximise shareholder returns

questions.explanation: Ethics and sustainability are closely linked: both require decision-makers to consider the interests of others and the long-term consequences of their actions. Ethical business practices can help anticipate risks to the organisation and the wider environment. A responsible approach to sustainability is therefore part of behaving ethically.

questions.topic: The concept of ethics and its significance for the accountancy profession
questions.question_text: Which of the following is most important in establishing an ethical culture within an organisation?

options.A: Rewarding staff solely on short-term sales targets
options.B: Keeping the code of conduct confidential to the board
options.C: Discouraging staff from raising concerns
options.D: Senior management consistently demonstrating ethical behaviour ('tone at the top')

questions.explanation: An ethical culture depends heavily on leaders setting an example through their own behaviour. This is supported by a published code of conduct, training, reward systems that do not encourage unethical behaviour, and safe channels for raising concerns. Narrow sales-based rewards and discouraging concerns tend to undermine ethical culture.

questions.topic: The concept of ethics and its significance for the accountancy profession
questions.question_text: When a professional accountant is making an ethical decision, why is it important to identify the stakeholders affected?

options.A: Because an ethical decision should consider how the outcome affects each affected party's interests, not just the interests of the decision-maker or their employer
options.B: Because the decision should always favour whichever stakeholder pays the accountant's fees
options.C: Because stakeholders must vote on every ethical decision
options.D: Because identifying stakeholders removes the need to apply the fundamental principles

questions.explanation: Ethical decision-making involves identifying who will be affected and weighing their interests, including the public interest. This helps the accountant see the full consequences of options and avoid decisions that serve only narrow interests. Stakeholder analysis supports, but does not replace, the fundamental principles in the Code.

questions.topic: The concept of ethics and its significance for the accountancy profession
questions.question_text: A professional accountant in practice is asked to provide assurance on a client's greenhouse gas emissions statement. Which statement about the ethical requirements that apply is correct?

options.A: No ethical requirements apply because the engagement does not involve financial information
options.B: Only the principle of confidentiality applies, because emissions data is commercially sensitive
options.C: The fundamental principles and relevant independence requirements apply, just as they do to financial statement engagements
options.D: Ethical requirements apply only if the client is a listed company

questions.explanation: The ICAEW Code of Ethics applies to all professional activities of members, including sustainability engagements. Because this is an assurance engagement, independence requirements apply alongside the five fundamental principles. Ethical requirements do not depend on whether the subject matter is financial or on the client being listed.

questions.question_text: According to the ICAEW Code of Ethics, what is a distinguishing mark of the accountancy profession?

options.A: Its focus on maximising fee income
options.B: Its exclusive right to prepare all tax returns
options.C: Its duty to act only in the interests of the employing organisation
options.D: Its acceptance of the responsibility to act in the public interest

questions.explanation: The Code states that a distinguishing mark of the accountancy profession is its acceptance of the responsibility to act in the public interest. A professional accountant's responsibility is therefore not exclusively to satisfy the needs of an individual client or employer. This responsibility underpins public trust in the profession.

questions.question_text: In the context of governance, what does 'accountability' mean?

options.A: Keeping accurate accounting records
options.B: Having the right to make decisions without explanation
options.C: Publishing all information about a company, including trade secrets
options.D: Being answerable to others for decisions and actions, and accepting responsibility for their outcomes

questions.explanation: Accountability means that those with power, such as directors, must explain and justify their decisions to those they serve, such as shareholders and other stakeholders, and accept responsibility for the results. Keeping records supports accountability but is not the same thing. Accountability is the opposite of making decisions without explanation.

questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes 'transparency' in corporate governance?

options.A: Using glass walls in office buildings
options.B: Reporting only positive results to shareholders
options.C: Making all decisions in private board meetings
options.D: Openness and clarity in disclosing information, so that stakeholders can understand the organisation's decisions and performance

questions.explanation: Transparency is about open, clear and timely disclosure of relevant information, both positive and negative. It allows stakeholders to hold the organisation to account and supports trust. Selective disclosure of good news only undermines transparency.

questions.question_text: The UK Cadbury Report (1992) gave a widely used definition of corporate governance. What is it?

options.A: The process by which a company calculates its tax liability
options.B: The system by which companies are directed and controlled
options.C: The set of accounting standards a company must follow
options.D: The method by which share prices are determined

questions.explanation: The Cadbury Report defined corporate governance as 'the system by which companies are directed and controlled'. Boards of directors are responsible for the governance of their companies, and shareholders appoint the directors and auditors to satisfy themselves that an appropriate governance structure is in place.

questions.question_text: Why are independent non-executive directors considered important to good governance?

options.A: They manage the day-to-day operations of the business
options.B: They can provide objective challenge to executive management and help protect the interests of shareholders and other stakeholders
options.C: They prepare the company's statutory financial statements
options.D: They guarantee that the company will make a profit

questions.explanation: Independent non-executive directors are not involved in day-to-day management, which allows them to scrutinise and challenge executives objectively. They often sit on audit, remuneration and nomination committees. This supports ethical behaviour and reduces the risk of management acting in its own interests.

questions.question_text: Shareholders own a company but appoint directors to run it. The directors award themselves large bonuses linked to short-term profits, at the expense of long-term value. Which concept does this illustrate?

options.A: The tragedy of the commons
options.B: The agency problem
options.C: Professional scepticism
options.D: The circular economy

questions.explanation: The agency problem arises when agents (directors) act in their own interests rather than in the interests of the principals (shareholders) who appointed them. Governance mechanisms such as independent boards, well-designed remuneration and transparent reporting aim to reduce this conflict.

questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes professional scepticism?

options.A: An attitude that includes a questioning mind, being alert to conditions that may indicate misstatement, and critical assessment of evidence
options.B: Assuming that management is dishonest in every engagement
options.C: Accepting all information provided by a client as reliable
options.D: Refusing to rely on any evidence unless it is obtained from a third party

questions.explanation: Professional scepticism means maintaining a questioning mind and critically assessing evidence, without assuming either dishonesty or unquestioned honesty. It helps accountants to identify errors, bias and fraud. Automatically assuming dishonesty or rejecting all client evidence would be unbalanced and impractical.

questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes professional judgement?

options.A: Following rules mechanically without considering the facts
options.B: Doing whatever the client's management prefers
options.C: Making decisions based purely on personal intuition without regard to standards
options.D: The application of relevant training, knowledge and experience to make informed decisions about the appropriate course of action in the circumstances

questions.explanation: Professional judgement involves applying knowledge, skills and experience, together with an understanding of the facts and relevant standards, to reach well-reasoned decisions. It is especially important under a principles-based code, where not every situation is covered by a specific rule.

questions.question_text: An accountant reviewing a provision estimate starts from last year's figure and makes only small adjustments, even though circumstances have changed significantly. Which type of bias is this most likely to be?

options.A: Automation bias
options.B: Groupthink
options.C: Anchoring bias
options.D: Availability bias

questions.explanation: Anchoring bias is the tendency to rely too heavily on an initial piece of information, such as last year's figure, when evaluating subsequent information. The accountant should reassess the estimate based on current evidence. Automation bias relates to over-reliance on systems, and groupthink to group decision-making.

questions.question_text: A finance manager believes that a new product has been a success. When reviewing sales data, she focuses on the regions with strong sales and pays little attention to regions where sales have been poor. Which bias is she showing?

options.A: Anchoring bias
options.B: Overconfidence bias
options.C: Confirmation bias
options.D: Automation bias

questions.explanation: Confirmation bias is the tendency to favour information that supports an existing belief and to underweight information that contradicts it. Recognising this bias helps accountants seek out and consider evidence fairly, which is essential for informed judgements and reliable communication with stakeholders.

questions.question_text: An assistant accepts the output of a spreadsheet-based forecasting tool without question, even though some results look unusual, because 'the system is always right'. Which bias does this demonstrate?

options.A: Automation bias
options.B: Confirmation bias
options.C: Selective perception
options.D: Representation bias

questions.explanation: Automation bias is the tendency to favour output generated from automated systems, even when human reasoning or contradictory information suggests it may be unreliable. Accountants should understand the limits of the tools they use and challenge unexpected results.

questions.question_text: A board consistently reaches quick unanimous decisions and members are reluctant to challenge the chief executive. Which of the following would be most effective in reducing the risk of groupthink?

options.A: Requiring all decisions to be made more quickly
options.B: Restricting board papers so that only the chief executive sees full information
options.C: Appointing only directors who share the chief executive's views
options.D: Inviting independent members to challenge proposals and asking for alternative options to be considered before decisions are made

questions.explanation: Groupthink occurs when the desire for harmony leads a group to reach decisions without critically evaluating alternatives. It can be reduced by encouraging diverse views, independent challenge, considering alternatives and ensuring all members have full information. The other options would make groupthink worse.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a likely consequence for the accountancy profession as a whole when a professional accountant is found to have acted unethically?

options.A: Higher fees for all accountants
options.B: Removal of the need for audit
options.C: Automatic tax relief for clients
options.D: Loss of public trust and confidence in the profession

questions.explanation: Unethical conduct by individuals damages the reputation of the whole profession and undermines public trust, which can lead to tighter external regulation. For the individual, consequences can include disciplinary action, fines and loss of membership. Organisations may suffer financial losses and reputational damage.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is part of ICAEW's regulatory role in maintaining public trust?

options.A: Setting the rates of UK income tax
options.B: Investigating complaints about members and firms and taking disciplinary action where appropriate
options.C: Prosecuting criminal offences in the courts
options.D: Appointing the directors of listed companies

questions.explanation: ICAEW acts as a regulator of its members and firms, including monitoring firms, investigating complaints and taking disciplinary action. These measures help ensure that members comply with professional standards. Setting tax rates, prosecuting criminal offences and appointing directors are not ICAEW's role.

questions.question_text: A student member of ICAEW is unsure how to respond to an ethical dilemma at work and wants confidential advice. Which ICAEW resource would be most appropriate?

options.A: The company's external auditors
options.B: A social media discussion group
options.C: The local newspaper
options.D: ICAEW's ethics advisory service (helpline)

questions.explanation: ICAEW provides a confidential ethics advisory service to help members and students apply the Code of Ethics to their circumstances. Discussing a client or employer issue on social media or with the press could breach confidentiality, and the external auditors are not the appropriate source of personal ethical advice.

questions.question_text: What is a key advantage of a principles-based code of ethics, such as the ICAEW Code, compared with a rules-based code?

options.A: It gives a precise answer for every possible situation
options.B: It removes the need for professional judgement
options.C: It allows accountants to do anything not specifically prohibited
options.D: It can be applied to new or unusual situations that specific rules do not anticipate

questions.explanation: A principles-based code sets out fundamental principles and a conceptual framework that can be applied to any situation, including ones not foreseen when the code was written. It requires professional judgement. A rules-based code can encourage a 'tick-box' approach and the view that anything not expressly prohibited is acceptable.

questions.question_text: Which statement best describes the relationship between the IESBA Code of Ethics, the ICAEW Code of Ethics and the FRC Ethical Standard?

options.A: The ICAEW Code is based on the IESBA Code with some additional requirements, while the FRC Ethical Standard sets requirements for auditors and other assurance practitioners in the UK that can be more restrictive
options.B: The IESBA Code applies only in the UK and replaces both the ICAEW Code and the FRC Ethical Standard
options.C: The FRC Ethical Standard applies to all accountants in business, whereas the ICAEW Code applies only to auditors
options.D: The three codes are unrelated and frequently contradict each other

questions.explanation: The IESBA Code is the international code issued by the International Ethics Standards Board for Accountants, and the ICAEW Code is derived from it with some additional UK requirements. The FRC Ethical Standard applies to audit and certain other assurance engagements in the UK and can impose stricter requirements, particularly on independence. Where both apply, the auditor must follow the more restrictive requirement.

questions.question_text: An accountant faces a situation that is not specifically addressed anywhere in the ICAEW Code of Ethics. What should the accountant do?

options.A: Conclude that, because there is no specific rule, any course of action is acceptable
options.B: Wait until a specific rule is issued before acting
options.C: Follow whatever approach their employer prefers
options.D: Apply the conceptual framework to identify, evaluate and address any threats to compliance with the fundamental principles

questions.explanation: The ICAEW Code is principles-based. Where no specific requirement exists, the accountant must still comply with the fundamental principles by applying the conceptual framework: identifying threats, evaluating them, and addressing them by eliminating them or reducing them to an acceptable level. The absence of a rule does not make any action acceptable.

questions.question_text: An accountant knowingly signs off a report that contains a misleading statement about stock levels. Which fundamental principle has been breached most directly?

options.A: Confidentiality
options.B: Integrity
options.C: Professional competence and due care
options.D: Objectivity

questions.explanation: Integrity requires accountants to be straightforward and honest in all professional and business relationships. They must not knowingly be associated with information containing materially false or misleading statements. Knowingly signing a misleading report is therefore a breach of integrity.

questions.question_text: An accountant is asked to evaluate a supplier tender in which her brother is one of the bidders. Which fundamental principle is most at risk?

options.A: Confidentiality
options.B: Objectivity
options.C: Professional behaviour
options.D: Professional competence and due care

questions.explanation: Objectivity requires accountants to exercise professional judgement without being compromised by bias, conflict of interest or undue influence of others. A close family relationship with a bidder creates a risk that her judgement will be biased. She should disclose the relationship and withdraw from the evaluation.

questions.question_text: A newly qualified accountant is asked to prepare complex group consolidation adjustments involving foreign subsidiaries, which she has never done before, with no supervision and a tight deadline. Which fundamental principle is most at risk?

options.A: Integrity
options.B: Professional competence and due care
options.C: Objectivity
options.D: Confidentiality

questions.explanation: Professional competence and due care requires accountants to attain and maintain the knowledge and skill needed for the work, and to act diligently in accordance with applicable standards. Taking on unfamiliar complex work without support or time risks a breach. She should request supervision, training or more time, or decline the work.

questions.question_text: At a dinner party, an accountant tells friends about the financial difficulties of a well-known local business that is one of her firm's clients. Which fundamental principle has she breached?

options.A: Confidentiality
options.B: Objectivity
